utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances today, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, Ms. Tatjana Savic, and Dan Beauchemin appearing for the Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Mr. Krgovic and Miroslav Cuskic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Last week we had indicated that the summary of a ruling that we had delivered would be followed by a fuller oral ruling, which we now deliver. The Trial Chamber now provides reasons for its ruling on the 10th of January, 2011, denying the Prosecution's motion of the 23rd of November, 2010. In this motion the Prosecution had requested reconsideration of the Trial Chamber's 4th of November, 2010, oral ruling admitting into evidence certain unsigned statements, referred to as "Official Notes." The Defence jointly responded on 3rd of December, 2010, objecting to the motion. The Prosecution argued that the Trial Chamber admitted the Official Notes "for the truth of their contents." It submits that the ruling was made "without an adequate finding of reliability of voluntariness" thus contravening Rules 89(C) and 95. For these reasons, it submitted, the ruling must be reconsidered. Alternatively, in order to challenge the reliability of the Official Notes, the Prosecution sought to add ST-238 to its Rule 65 ter witness list and sought to expand the scope of ST-228's testimony. The Trial Chamber recalls that it did not admit the Official Notes for the truth of the matters asserted therein. Instead it admitted the documents as evidence of the procedures followed by the investigators at the Omarska camp while interrogating detainees and as proof of what the investigators noted the detainees' declarations to be, not as free and voluntary statements of the detainees themselves. The Chamber also held that the issue of what weight to be assigned to the contents, as outlined above, will remain a task for the Trial Chamber at the end of the trial. For these reasons, the Trial Chamber denied the motion in its entirety. Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to inform Your Honours in respect of the witness who was here before Christmas was ill and never testified, Your Honours, I am -- apologise, it's actually not much to do with the Prosecution as such, but it appears now that having organised a videolink from his country of residence, the witness yesterday faxed to VWS a medical certificate which asserts that he is able to travel, and he is very anxious to give evidence in person. In those circumstances, we feel that it's only right and proper that rather than going to the expense and trouble of a videolink, that the witness should be here to testify in person on Monday, and those are the arrangements that have been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So formally, I suppose, it is necessary for us to -- to reverse the order that we would have made permitting the videolink, and, as I recall, the issue was canvassed yesterday as to moving Monday's session to the afternoon to accommodate a technician who had to travel. So we would remain on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I had no idea there was any such canvassing going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It may have been out of -- I remember --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- it was discussed but it may very well have been out of court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, Your Honours know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I am reminded that it was in fact in court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It completely escaped me. But, anyway, Your Honours, no, he will be here, I believe, on Sunday and so he can testify on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have a matter, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I was -- I stood up [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... could the witness be escorted to the stand. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brown. Whereas you probably think that - and I would be inclined to agree - it's otiose, I am obliged to remind you that you are still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have a few more documents to show you related to the same topic that we discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D266, which is Defence tab 129.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, that is one of the documents that you received yesterday during the break. It has been printed for you. This is yet another order by the commander of Tactical Group 3, Colonel Lisica. The date is the 11 November 1992 and it says here order for the engagement of units of the Doboj CSB and the SJB Doboj. And it goes on to say: "Based on demonstrated need, I hereby order, number 1, 100 policemen shall be selected by the SJB Doboj," and then it goes on to give a specific task that they should carry out. And under item number 3, Colonel Lisica says that for the execution of this order Andrija Bjelosevic, the CSB chief, and Obren Petrovic, the SJB chief, shall be personally responsible to him. Do you remember, Mr. Brown, and you will certainly agree with me, that this is a clear-cut case of a subordination of the police to the military?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At face value it would seem that that is the case. Whether there is some agreement prior to this or whether Colonel Lisica was operating in some other way, I don't know. Whether this was referring to exceptional circumstances at the front or any other agreement, I'm not sure. I would have to see other documents surrounding that. But, at face value, this document does appear to say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you can see under number 3 that the commander, Colonel Lisica, says that the people from the police will be personally responsible for the execution of this order, the CSB chief and the SJB chief. If there was some sort of an agreement, I'm sure that this order would not contain this item.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't necessarily agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document has been MFI'd, and I propose to make it a proper exhibit, if there are no objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours it's the same objection as yesterday. This whole series of documents to do with Lisica and Bjelosevic, we're asking for the proper provenance of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, can I just finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The second matter is this. The witness has done no more -- this could have been shown to another witness. I'm not sure whether it was or not, nor am I sure why it was MFI'd at the time, but this witness can't say anything except, "I see what it says here."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yesterday, after the end of the session, my whole team made an effort to re-check once again whether some of the documents that I want to go through with this document -- with this witness is, indeed, yes. This document, for which Ms. Korner says it has no provenance, is in EDS. It's number 06201475. So the reason that this document was MFI'd was her objection that this document doesn't have proper provenance. However, it is obvious that this document was in the hands of the Prosecution, because it's in EDS. EDS is a place where the Prosecution puts documents. That's why I think that the situation is simple and that MFI designation can now be dropped and this can become a proper exhibit. Maybe the usher could help so Ms. Korner can see the document. There is also the ERN number, and I think that it is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So do I understand that this is not in the category of -- of the document such as we discussed yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I -- I -- I don't think it's in a category since it is in the electronic database of this Tribunal. So, therefore, the provenance is from -- from this Tribunal. If -- if Ms. Korner will maintain her -- her opposition or -- or suggestion that we should now find out how this document was uploaded into the EDS, well, then -- then I guess it would be the same situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've checked and that's right. So the basis of my first part of my objection is not right. I'm not clear why it was MFI'd last time but I don't think it was anything to do with me, but in any event that's absolutely right. So from that basis we do -- it appears we seize this document, although there was nothing to indicate that on the copy that we were provided with, in which case my objection obviously doesn't stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And in terms of your second objection, it seems to me that the stage we're at in the Prosecution's case, this being the last-but-one witness, and it's a document on which the Defence wishes to rely, we may as well admit it at this stage. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So, it is my understanding that the document is de-MFI'd?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a brief observation. This document belongs to the same group of documents, those which were received from Republika Srpska. We discussed it yesterday. We received it from the government, or, rather, republican secretariat of Republika Srpska. So it's the same group of documents. We were lucky enough to find this particular document inside EDS, but I'm rather certain that all other documents that we used yesterday are also in EDS. I'm going to return to this topic once I'm able to make additional checks as to what is exactly in EDS. Can we now have 1D00-0345.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is another document by Mr. Lisica. I assume it is related to the previous document, because it has the same date. It's tab 130. The commander, Colonel Lisica, here orders to form a mixed battalion as follows: A company of military police and a Doboj police company and another police company from Teslic. And he appoints as the commander the SJB chief, and as a deputy a lieutenant, which means a military person. Then under number 3, he defines the task, and further on says readiness for the attack at 0700 hours on 12th November, 1992. Sir, again, there is no doubt that this is a resubordination of the police to the military because Colonel Lisica here even appoints as the commander of this newly formed unit the CSB chief from Doboj?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would appear to be issuing an order for a joint operation in that area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But a joint operation is under his command, isn't it? It's not a joint operation by the police and the military. Here the police is resubordinated, a commander of the new mixed unit is appointed, and it is to him that Colonel Lisica ordered what to do and when to do it, right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a joint operation in that there is military and civilian police but I would accept that, yes, he is instructing as you -- as you indicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the joint operation cannot be if it's the case of resubordination. We have to agree about one thing. I hope that you will agree with me that when members of the police are resubordinated to the army, they lose, first, their status of authorised officials; and, secondly, they gain the same rights and duties as any other military conscript. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would ask you to show me references that that is the case, because I have not seen that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when I show you regulations, you tell me that are you not an expert for legal issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, he has been asked -- either Mr. Zecevic shows him or he doesn't. He has been asked by the witness to show them. He can't make comments like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, if I were to show you relevant legislation on which I base this particular claim of mine, would it help?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We are going to prepare this, and I'm going to hand it over to you. Sir, if the commander, Slavko Lisica, ordered, first, to form a mixed battalion; then he, de facto, brought the members of the military and the members of the police into one unit, he appointed the commander of that unit, he gave them a task, and he also determined the place and the time of the attack, and now you tell me that this is a joint operation. And I put it to you that in this particular case, the police has been resubordinated to the army and there is no joint operation. This is a military unit carrying out tasks defined by the commander of the tactical group.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a joint operation in that there's a civilian and police component. That's what I mean by joint operation. But I agree with you that at face value this document, Colonel Lisica clearly believes he has the authority to issue an order in order to place police under his command, and he issues an instruction in that respect. And I accept that that seems to be at face value what this document says. The background to the operation, why that happened, any agreements that may have come or his belief about why he could do that is something I can't comment. But at face value, this document does appear to say that, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, thank you for your answer. Now, a general question. So let us disregard this particular example. When a member of the police is resubordinated to a military commander, and you told us that this is possible to happen in the British Army as well, although in exceptional cases. Then, do those members of the police remain members of the police, or do they become members of the military from that moment on, the moment of resubordination?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They remain members of the police who happen to be -- but conducting tasks with the military and placed under their command, in that exceptional circumstance. But they remain a member of the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You really surprise me with this answer. If a member of the police is resubordinated to the army, then he cannot be member of the police anymore. Because, from that moment on, his superior officer from the police cannot command him. He is from that point on commanded by a military officer. That's the whole essence of the concept of resubordination, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it doesn't follow that just because for a particular or exceptional operation a police -- policeman or a police unit is placed under a military command that they lose or suddenly become, in essence, members of the army or that they lose their position within the police force. In exceptional circumstances what normally would happen is once the operation is finished they go back to doing what they normally do as policemen. They don't suddenly chop and change. In my experience, when policemen are subordinated in exceptional circumstances they don't suddenly become in essence soldiers and lose or change in an instant only to change back later. They remain within the police. And that would seem to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, please focus on my question. I said during the time of resubordination, whether it's one day or three months or two years, doesn't matter, but during the resubordination to the military command. Now you're telling me that this person in British Army remains a policeman regardless of the fact that he had been resubordinated to the military and that he receives his orders from the military. Is that what you're telling me?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my experience, yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then can you explain to me whether this member of the military who is actually a policeman resubordinated to the British Army for a particular operation, if he sees a case of theft that occurred during this operation, does it mean that he still has duties and obligations as a member of the police and then he has to pursue that thief and arrest him or he has to stay in his formation and wait for orders to -- for orders being issued by the military commander, the commander to whom he had been resubordinated. What is he to do in this situation?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would expect that he has obligations as a policeman and he presumably has obligations within any chain of command within the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Brown, these two things are mutually exclusive. The military commander tells him, Stand here and guard this, say, passage; and if somebody comes along shoot him. And, at the same time, his duty as a policeman is to go and arrest a perpetrator of a criminal offence. So he has to do either one or the other. What is a British policeman resubordinated to the military command going to do, one or the other? He cannot do both. You have to give me your answer. What is your opinion? What is this person going to do?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not really quite clear on the question, I have to say. To be -- to be quite honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think that I haven't added anything to my question that I asked you before and you gave the answer to that question, but you didn't give a proper answer. I asked you one or the other, and you told me both. Does that mean that you don't have an opinion on this issue, or -- or you don't know the answer?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand your question. All I can say is that -- that normally in my experience when police officers are subordinated to the military, there is a planning process under which the -- that subordination occurs with the limitations or expanse of that subordination. But a policeman who is subordinated for a particular task in the military, to my knowledge, remains a policeman, operates under his -- his -- his regulations, and would be briefed up and made aware of the regulations he was -- he was operating whilst he was attached to the military. But he doesn't lose his status as a policeman. That's, from my experience, what happens. And that goes with -- with other subordinations. There's an -- there is invariably some agreement prior to the subordination about the limits or expanses of that subordination. Some of those can be simple issues of logistics, some of those can be issues of discipline. But, in my experience, when police are working under the military, if that is the case, they don't suddenly, in essence just become soldiers for that period, subject to army law, and able to be tasked exclusively by commanders and to operate under commanders. They remain as police officers. And I would imagine -- I'm not an expert on the British police, but they have obligations to uphold law and protect citizens and the usual tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If your point, sir, is that when a policeman is subordinated to the military to all intents and purpose they become a soldier, full stop, I would not agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] okay, fair enough. [Interpretation] I accept that you're unwilling to agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I object to the comments like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot see anything wrong with my comment. I just said that the witness was unwilling to agree with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry but it's a comment, and I repeat for about the third time: Cross-examination is asking questions of the witness, not making comments. Comments are final address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Let's move on, shall we?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D410, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, during your examination-in-chief, you commented on document P1668 which is tab 56 of the Prosecution and your footnote is 329, and 355 is the other footnote. You commented on this letter written by the commander, corps commander General Talic, and it is about the engagement of the unit in late November at the Posavina front. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you characterised it as a request, submitted by Talic with which I disagree, since the request is about the acceleration of the preparation and not about the engagement of police units. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I do think it's a request or he is asking him to -- to prepare and organise the police units of at least two battalions in accordance with an expressed -- an expressed need. Presumably there's been some prior discussion or expression of this need.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this document makes no mention of any previous consultation or agreement. It seems that no one document that I showed you and -- but -- and which was explicit about resubordination where you did not suggest that there must have been some sort of agreement or something of that kind although no indication of that was found in any of those documents. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think paragraph 1 says in accordance with the expressed needs, General Talic has clearly expressed a requirement or a need have this additional support. It doesn't say whether that was in a meeting, in an instruction, in a discussion, but I would take it from the first line that General Talic has --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Has a need.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- has expressed a need to have this additional support.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with that. After that document, on the following day we saw 2D119 which is an order by Mr. Zupljanin about raising men for the unit to be sent to the front which is tab -- tab 57, but there's no reason to display that document now. In essence, sir, when those two battalions, police battalions, arrived on the 23rd or 24th of November in Banja Luka, because they had come from the entire territory of the Krajina, because we're speaking about a large number of police officers, two battalions after all, at that moment, a police brigade was established. General Talic greeted them and appointed the commander of that brigade. We even saw a video here. I don't know if you had the chance to see the video recording of that parade when the brigade commander, Mr. Peulic was appointed. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen that video, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But you do know that General Talic appointed the commander of that brigade and that commander was Colonel Peulic.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that, sir. The document, on 22nd November, doesn't indicate that Peulic is the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me show you the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2D118, which is tab 5 of the Zupljanin Defence. Mr. Krgovic kindly let me have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't expect that you wouldn't know that, so I didn't prepare for this. I apologise. But here's the document. There is obviously a mistake with the dates because the year is 1993, which we can tell from the incoming mail stamp, so the 2nd of January 1992 is not the correct date. And here, the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, Momir Talic, orders that Colonel Dragoslav Djurkic be the commander of the police brigade; whereas, the previous commander, Bosko Peulic is returned to his previous duties. The handover of duties shall be completed no later than 4 January 1993. Have you seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't know then that the police brigade in the Bosnian theatre was commanded by Bosko Peulic until another officer was appointed commander of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that sir. I know that the initial establishment in November, end of November, had a different commander. Whether there was a decision that, as this brigade was going to be going into the corridor, a military officer might be more beneficial and Colonel Peulic was placed in that position, I don't know. But I wasn't aware that Colonel Peulic was the commander of this or appointed as the commander of this, nor was I aware of what agreements may have been entered into in order for that to occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand what you say -- what you mean when you say that initially it had a different commander. When it was lined up for the first time in Banja Luka, the police brigade I mean, when it was established, then General Talic arrived and we saw the video, that's a Prosecution Exhibit. But I hope my learned friend will let me have it so I can show it to you. And General Talic appointed Bosko Peulic commander of that brigade on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If it's an exhibit. If Mr. Zecevic wants to show it he can call it up. I can't remember what the number is, but I'm sure his team can tell him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm surprised that the gentleman who was an OTP expert has not seen the video, but we'll prepare it now and we can show it in a couple of minutes and so acquaint the expert with these facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, again it's an improper remark, but as Mr. Zecevic knows that video was only obtained very, very recently indeed, so it's not surprising that Mr. Brown, who has not been a member of the OTP for some years now, has not seen the video. If I had shown him every piece of evidence that we had obtained in the last few years, he would have been here for a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I -- I meant no evil and I really wasn't aware that the video was only subsequently ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, is it necessary to show the video. The witness didn't know that Peulic was commanding the brigade but he isn't challenging it as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Your Honours, it was not my intention to show the video or these documents because I thought it was an undisputed fact. However, the witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is undisputed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think it is, yes. It is undisputed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm just checking. I mean, certainly there is no question it was Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic who commanded the brigade. What I need to check is whether that was the -- it was originally intended that he or somebody else should do it. But certainly he was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am really am a bit confused. A short while ago the witness confirmed that according to his knowledge the initial commander of that unit was another person and that was my question to him. I'll give you the reference. I can refer to the transcript. Page 17, lines 6 and 7, the witness's answer was the following: "I know that the initial establishment in November, end of November, had a different commander."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, from the establishment document from the CSB on the 22nd November, Bosko Peulic is not annotated down as the commander. Now whether that was, you know, a decision after that, Colonel Peulic should be -- maybe it was more skilled or -- should be in there, or whether General Talic decided to appoint him. I don't know. I take it very much at face value that Colonel Peulic was the commander. I've not seen the video and so I don't contest that at all. But the document on the 22nd November outlining the -- which followed from that document which is seen, outlining all the individuals and the structure of that brigade has a Brane Pecanac as the commander. There may well have been that what happened is there was a decision to change that. That's all I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, when police units are resubordinated, they are resubordinated in an organised manner. In other words, the police officer is in charge of that unit. At the moment of resubordination to the military he, as commander of the unit, and the whole unit are resubordinated to the military and become part of the military establishment, military structure. Document 2D119 shows that the brigade command was appointed by the MUP, but that doesn't mean a thing, because their commander is appointed by the military because that unit is resubordinated to the military and that unit is commanded by a military officer. You know that Bosko Peulic is a military officer rather than a police officer correct -- am I right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely I know he was a military officer. But my point is that, and I have so say that I'm not an expert in the workings of the police brigade in the corridor in November and onwards, but it would seem that there was an express need by General Talic which necessitated him making requests to have this battalion or brigade formed. That was accepted by the CSB, and what the CSB did was that they organised the structure of that brigade as outlined in document D119 giving the whole structure of that brigade and the command component and, at least at face value from the document, appointing Brane Pecanac as the commander of the brigade. Now what happened after that to make Colonel Peulic the commander of the brigade, I do not know, and I take it at face value that there was that change or that there was an appointment, but I don't know. All I'm saying is that according to the document the CSB wrote, Colonel Peulic was not at least the initial commander or at least according to that -- that individual document. But as -- again, I'm not an expert on the police battalion structure. [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, can I interrupt because really I think it's only fair to the witness. The witness, having looked at the document, it's 2D119, and I think it should be put up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am not trying to impeach document 2D119, but I do object to the way Ms. Korner interferes with my examination of the witness. The witness and I absolutely agree on the contents of document 2D119. There is no dispute there. That's why I haven't shown it to the witness. By the way, the witness has it in front of him anyway. But what is in dispute is the issue of resubordination of this police brigade to the military. That is the crucial issue I'm discussing with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, if General Talic appointed a military officer, a lieutenant-colonel, Bosko Peulic, commander of this brigade, is this an instance of resubordination of this brigade, to your mind then? Resubordination to the military, that is.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be. But it could also be that the brigade lacked certain skills and General Talic has offered Colonel Peulic up as the commander. I don't doubt that if General Talic believes there's an exceptional need to have a police brigade for operations in the corridor that that brigade is to operate under his -- his corps. But clearly there's been significant discussion, agreement, acceptance, consensus involving the Ministry of Interior, the Krajina Corps, the CSB for this brigade to be -- to be formed and dispatched to the corps. When it's there, I don't doubt that it would have been subordinated to the corps for operations there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Brown, on page 21, line 18 you said that there's been significant discussion, agreement, acceptance, consensus involving the Ministry of the Interior. We have seen two documents: General Talic's request, and Mr. Zupljanin's order, which issued in his capacity as CSB chief. These are the only two documents you cite in your report concerning this matter. And, on the basis of these documents, you were unable to determine whether there was discussion, agreement, and so on. You may be able to assume that there was something of that kind, but I'm sure you cannot claim it for certain.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, I wasn't there, so I can't say for certain. But the document -- document says in accordance with an order from the minister of the interior on the basis of dispatch from the 1st Krajina Corps with the consent of the minister of the interior and clearly this is a CSB Banja Luka instruction, so I would -- I would assume that -- that that constitutes some kind of process of agreement and consent that this -- and this occurs very quickly. The request is quite -- at least General Talic's instruction, I don't know what went on prior to that, but this seems to have happened quite swiftly, and we're talking about a large unit, and we're talking about units coming from all over the Krajina, and the brigade was formed. And was dispatched. Now when I put all that together, I can only assume that this sort of co-ordination was fairly significant and the dispatch of this brigade was quite significant. So I may be wrong. I wasn't there. I don't know what meetings were there, but my feeling is that with that background that that type of consent was -- was agreed and accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, you confirmed yesterday that you hadn't seen the minister's orders. When I showed you an order of the minister, and we had -- we had to print them during the break for you to review these documents for the first time, the minister's order dated 15 May was at stake, and we're talking about November. The minister's order is a legal text. That's why things go so fast, because under the law, that is the procedure. The police can be resubordinated to the military for the execution of combat missions and that is why these things were done so efficiently, because it's a legal obligation and it is set down by the law. Apart from all these matters you discussed with Ms. Korner, my learned friend asked you during the examination-in-chief some questions about discipline. And then to her question you said that you had never seen a document confirming the assumption that resubordinated MUP officers can be held accountable before military disciplinary or judiciary bodies. Do you remember confirming that to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I take that that's what I said. I -- I would accept that I haven't seen documents that -- to that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In your report, sir, item 249, and footnote 354, you cite a document which I would like to show you. It's 1D04-9050, tab 12. I hope it is not in dispute that you have seen this document earlier, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not the correct document in English. 1D04-9050. The Serbian original is right but the English translation is wrong. The tab number is 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's 1D049054, tab 12. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you must have seen this document before, since it appears in your footnote 354, right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen it. I remember it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document of the 1st Krajina Corps. It was not signed by Major-General Momir Talic but by one of his assistants because it says "for the commander?" Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this is about police members abandoning their positions; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would appear to be, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And it says in paragraph 2: "Immediately file criminal reports for each individual and take other measures to inform the public," et cetera. "Immediately file criminal reports for each individual ..." Is that not implementing disciplinary or penal measures against these members by the military?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't accept that that's what's happening. I think what has happened is that the Krajina Corps has received this information from the Main Staff. They're quoting it and sending it directly to the CSB and with the intention that the CSB file criminal reports presumably in relation to the list of men who are included on this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute, Mr. Brown. This document was sent to the CSB Banja Luka to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps and the 43rd Motorised Brigade. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Korner, please be so kind as to get up and say whatever is that you have to say. Do not suggest anything in other ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this document is written by the command of the Krajina Corps. They're writing from the forward command post, and the document is being sent to the CSB of Banja Luka to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps and the 43rd Motorised Brigade; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would say that on the document, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So on of basis of what did you conclude that this had been sent to the CSB as an instruction for them to file criminal charges immediately? And in your view how is it that the 1st Krajina Corps command can order the CSB Banja Luka to file criminal charges against their members?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My reading of this is that the forward command post at this time, probably where General Talic was based, received some information from the Main Staff. General Talic or whoever signed the document on his behalf sends a copy of that to the 1st Krajina Corps, presumably for the archive, because that is where the headquarters was based. The 43rd brigade potentially, because maybe that was the unit that -- well, it comes from Prijedor, is related to the Prijedor area, and it sent it to the Banja Luka CSB. And I think it's sending it to the Banja Luka CSB because it expects the Banja Luka CSB to immediately file criminal charges on the individuals who fled. General Talic hasn't sent this to the military courts or to -- to -- to the military disciplinary organs. He sent it is to the CSB because I think that's where he expects individuals to take action against the policemen who fled the front line or whatever they've alleged to have done. Abandoned positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, it is certain that you did -- do not expect the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps to file criminal charges. He is telling his own subordinate units to do that; isn't that right? General Talic would not be signing criminal reports, would he? I hope that is not what you are trying to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is why I interrupted. I accept that the -- the criticism that I shouldn't have interrupted in the way I did. I do not know on what basis Mr. Zecevic is asserting that this is not sent to the CSB for it to prosecute as Mr. Brown has said. If he has a reason for asserting it, I think that ought to be put.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All in due time, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brown, please reply to my question. I have put a question to you. Oh, the question was whether you expect General Talic to be signing criminal reports or do you expect General Talic to tell his subordinate units, or rather, instruct them to file criminal reports against members of the military who had abandoned their positions.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If your assertion is that General Talic is sending this to the Banja Luka CSB and by sending that document that implies the Banja Luka CSB is a subordinate unit to the corps, I would disagree with you. General Talic, if he himself or his staff are made aware of criminal charges of military figures in his command, I would expect him to initiate a process to -- of -- of filing criminal charges through the military judicial process. But, as I say, I think this is a document that is sent to the Banja Luka CSB in the expectation that they should investigate what had happened to individuals, individual policemen, and that -- that to me is what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Brown, you will agree that it would be most logical for military conscripts who abandoned their positions have their direct superiors, the commanding officers of the units that they were in before they had abandoned their positions would file criminal reports? I'm talking about military conscripts. It should be done by their direct commanding officers, not the corps commander, right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I guess if the corps commander receives information, which, in this case, has happened through the Main Staff it could be initiated by the corps commander. But if -- if conscripts from a battalion or a brigade fled, you would expect the battalion to -- to initiate the investigation process.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me something else. If that were true, actually I don't want to speculate any further. Tell me just one thing. It is a fact that as far as military conscripts are concerned, it is the military judicial that is in charge, right? For as long as they're in the army. Do we agree on that at least?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's the case. And I believe that was the case in the RS Law on the Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, have a look at what it says here in this document. "Attachment: List of military conscripts," that's what I'd like to highlight, "reserve policemen who fled from their positions." Mr. Brown, that is why I'm putting this to you, that Commander Momir Talic is hereby ordering military units to file criminal charges because he is acting the right way in accordance with the law. He is treating reserve policemen who had been resubordinated to the military as military conscripts. There's 71 of them, and, therefore, they have to be held accountable before military courts because, as military conscripts, they are responsible, not as policemen. Because they abandoned a military unit. Do you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's take things one at a time then. What is it that you disagree with? Do you disagree with me saying that they are military conscripts? These reserve policemen. Are they military conscripts or not? Yes or no. [In English] It's a simple question, Mr. Brown. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know from the attachment whether they are policemen or whether they are conscripts, whether they're members of the 43rd Brigade, soldiers, or whatever. If all of them are policemen --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, Mr. Brown, please, we are looking at a document, both you and I are looking at this document. So far, you have been making the following assertion to me. Since the heading of the document says that members of the police had abandoned their positions, you were saying that General Talic is writing to the CSB Banja Luka and instructing them or suggesting to them that they should file criminal charges against their members. Now this is what I'm putting to that you, that that is not the case. That he is providing information to the CSB but that he is instructing his own subordinate units, the 43rd Motorised Brigade, first and foremost, to file criminal reports against these reserve policemen who had abandoned positions at a moment when they were resubordinated to the military. At that point in time, they were military conscripts and all of that is written in this document. Sir --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not my reading of the document, sir. My reading of the document, as I said before --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, it is the time that we would take a break. Could we resume this exercise in 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours may I just raise the question of timing. I'm a little concerned that we may not even finish Mr. Brown tomorrow morning. And, as you know, he is anxious to be able to leave tomorrow. I was wondering, just in case we could possibly make arrangements to maybe sit a little longer tomorrow. I don't know whether that affects Your Honours' abilities to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Today you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, either today or tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Registry would -- we would see whether we can do it tomorrow. It would be --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I hope it won't be necessary, Your Honours. But as it -- and can I say this not a criticism of Mr. Zecevic. I understand why this is going on a little longer, but it's just a question of having it available, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, do I understand that the witness would be available into the afternoon tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think so, Your Honour, yes. I think his problem is from tomorrow evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I see. Very well. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we will request the Registry to make arrangements, tentative, for a fourth session tomorrow to accommodate any possible spillover. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brown, I think that you said towards the end that did you not agree with the position that I presented in my last question; namely, that these are reserve policemen who had fled from their positions and that in this document the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps is treating them as military conscripts which is what is written in the document itself. I think that your answer to that question was not fully recorded.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the document at the end says list of conscripts, reserve policemen. But I think I made my position clear that I think General Talic believes that the Banja Luka CSB is to initiate proceedings against these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us now look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, are we going to leave this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, no, the second page of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ah, right. Thanks. I have a question relating to the document when you're finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, this is a list of these military conscripts as Mr. -- as General Momir Talic says, who had abandoned their positions. And this very list says "list of soldiers." I underline the word "soldiers," who wilfully abandoned their positions between 13th of September, 1992, and the 11th of October, 1992. Obviously, the command of the 1st Krajina Corps considers them to be soldiers; and if they consider them to be soldiers, as you said to me a moment ago, in that case, as for taking disciplinary action again them, or bringing criminal charges against them, it is the military commands that are in charge of that, and appropriate organs of the military judiciary, right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "soldiers" in the document. But if these individuals were soldiers, I would not have expected General Talic to send that to the CSB. There's no reference in this document to sending reports to the military police battalion, to the military courts, to the investigative military courts at all, and I stand by my position. I don't know why they've put "soldiers" on there, but it would seem to me that on face value this document is going to the CSB because they expect the CSB to initiate some kind of proceedings against them, or investigation, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I think it's quite clear that they are reserve policemen we saw that. Are you challenging the fact that the people on this list are reserve policemen?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if they are reserve policemen. I'm assuming they are because that's what the title of the document is about, so I'm not challenging that they're reserve policemen at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, you claim that General Talic is mistakenly calling them military conscripts on the first page and calling them soldiers on this list. Again, mistakenly. And that although they are military conscripts or soldiers, he is sending this to the CSB and expecting them to bring criminal charges against them. Is that your assertion?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My reading of this document is that these are reserve policemen who fled, the Main Staff has highlighted that, General Talic is sending this to the CSB in order for them to action it, and that as reserve policemen they don't fall within the Law on the Army or service rules and that's why he's sending them to the CSB. I think I've stated that a few times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How do you explain the fact that he is calling them soldiers?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't explain, whether it's an error whoever has made the list, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And at first he says military conscripts dash -- or, rather, comma, reserve policemen. Is that a mistake too, I assume?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say why they've put that, but the title of the document relates to reserve policemen, and I'm assuming that this list is of reserve policemen and the document is going to the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you keep forgetting that, on page 1 of this document, we see that this document was sent to the command of the 43rd Motorised Brigade and the command of the Krajina Corps. I think that we've already dealt with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, don't you think that this is as far as can you go with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I understand. Thank you very much. Your Honour, just for the record, one of the exhibits in this case is P1566. This the list of the -- the uncomplete list of the members of the reserve force of police in -- in Prijedor for September 1992, and I have identified during the break at least five of the persons which appear on the list in this document, this military document, which we are talking about. And I can give the references. Those are the numbers in this document which we are looking right now are numbers 22, 30, 62, 66, 70, and they correspond to numbers in P1566, 83, 104, 115, 85, and 142. And apparently, in addition, number 20, which corresponds to number 50 in this -- in this case. I'm notified that there are more, but I think this is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So, Mr. Zecevic, by this comparison, we are to conclude that the -- at least some of the persons there on the first lists we saw were, indeed, reserve police force members. Is that the conclusion that you are suggesting?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't -- I don't -- I don't -- I don't challenge that all of them are reserve policemen. What I'm saying is that the moment when they were resubordinated to the army, they lose their position as the police officers and became military conscripts, or soldiers, as the document says. That is the -- that this is the point. Your Honours, can I have this document admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, therefore, 1D04-9050 will become Exhibit 1D411.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I have a question for you and a question for the witness. My question to you is if you are in possession of any evidence that any of the persons, the 71 persons on the first list, were ever prosecuted; and, if they were, by which authority?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, not at this point, Your Honour, but I will gladly endeavour to find the documents in that -- in -- in relation to that, yes. If I can, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Of course, that goes without saying. But, of course, it would be interesting to see who actually took action on this, whether it would be the civilian prosecutor or the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: My question to the witness is this. What do you make of the fact that in the letter signed by someone in -- on behalf of General Talic, first of all, what do you make of the fact that this was brought to the level of Talic for him to sign the letter? Obviously someone else signed it on his behalf but it seem to me that under normal circumstances a -- an abandonment from the front line would be dealt with by the 43rd Corps itself. So my question is what are you able to infer from the fact that this was now brought to the level of the Main Staff of the Krajina Corps; secondly, what do you make of the fact that the Banja Luka CSB is indicated as the primary addressee of this letter? Is there any hierarchy to be inferred from the way in which the letter was drafted among the two addressees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly answering your first question, sir. It's clear that the flow of information has come from the Main Staff to the corps. That's -- I think it's not come from below to Talic. How the Main Staff got wind of that or under what process I'm not sure, but it seems that General Talic's headquarters has received the information so, in a way, I'm not surprised that General Talic is -- or him or his staff are dealing with it. That's one issue. And second, I think abandonment of a position is an important thing for a commander to know, irrespective of what level. I would, you know, commanders don't like to see that because it weakens their operations, their units. So in a way I don't see that in any surprising. In relation to the hierarchy, I can't say for sure but I would suspect that the CSB are number one because they are the ones who have to action it. I think the second distribution to the Krajina Corps headquarters is probably for the archive. I don't think the forward -- well, the forward command post did have an archive but it was a relatively small headquarters deployed to the corridor area to better manage the operations there. So I think the second distribution is probably for an archival purpose, and the 43rd Brigade may well have just been a unit that the soldiers abandoned and so it may be that General Talic is simply saying we're aware of this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. What you are suggesting, if I understand you correctly, is that the Banja Luka CSB is really the primary addressee and then the 43rd Motorised Brigade is copied for their information. Is that a correct understanding of what are you suggesting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Now I'm not sure where the Prijedor unit was, whether they actually abandoned from Prijedor or whether they're informing them because the 43rd brigade invariably covered Prijedor from its garrison. Well, that is my position, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If that is your suggestion, then my question is, if this letter were to be sent to the 43rd Motorised Brigade for their information, copied for their information, cc, however you want to put it, would that appear like this, or would -- would you not have expected that the authority to which this letter is sent for information would appear at the bottom of the page, normally? It would say cc 1st Krajina Corps, 43rd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The corps didn't seem to use that all the time, sir. I've seen instructions both with the distribution where it is here, and I've seen distributions in a long list at the bottom of the document. I'm not sure I can say one way or the other whether I would expect to see it on a document like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So your testimony is that it does occur frequently like this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've seen documents like this, yes, sir. It tends to be these smaller instructions, orders, information, where it's maybe one or two addressees get placed at the front. If it's a very large combat report that's going to every unit of the corps, it is often -- the distribution is often at the back of the document. But I've seen both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One question in relation to the question put by His Honour. Sir, you remember that yesterday we discussed document 1D368 that is your footnote 616. Tab 44. It has to do with guide-lines of the military prosecutor's office attached to the Main Staff of the army for setting the criteria for criminal prosecution. Do you remember that we commented on that document yesterday?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now can we have it on the screens. It's page 11, I think, or maybe 20. It 0760348. And at the beginning of the page is item 2. In the document itself, it's page 9. Yes, that's the page. They just tell me now that it's page 19. And in English, page 5. Sir, here, in item 2, it says: "The criminal offence of wilfully absenting one's self-from one's post and desertion from the armed forces - Article 217 of the Criminal Code." This relates to the topic we've just discussed, wilfully leaving the post -- I don't want to go into details. It's -- it has to do with the persons who took part that combat. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would imagine it covers combat as well. It may be wilfully abandoning your post in a way regarding a barracks or doing another military activity, but, yes, I think it is abandonment of a military position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You quoted this document in your report, footnote 616, so I think it isn't in dispute that this document envisages criminal offences. Those criminal offences which, in the view of the highest military prosecutor in the Army of Republika Srpska, the one attached to the Main Staff, would fall within the jurisdiction of the military judiciary. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For military personnel, and military personnel are defined in the service regulations as being members of the army, cadets, active and reserve army members, I think. I'm not a legal expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely; I agree with you. I have just a few more questions for you. I want to clarify some things in relation to some documents. Sir, in your report, in footnote 333A, that's the first footnote under the number 333, and you quote 1D04-9039, which is an order by the 5th Corps command dated 18th February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab number 9. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's one of the documents that was copied for you, I assume. Do you see the document?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Under (a), it says that: "Temporary check-points of the VP and the police shall be established to carry out thorough inspections of persons and vehicles entering and leaving and prevent any unauthorised circumstances and transport of military equipment" and other things. You can see that? I think that you used that in your report in order to illustrate some things that you were saying about the check-points.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think I would have to read my report again, but I think it was a document referring to joint police/military check-points. In this case, in Western Slavonia, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that in 1991, the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina carried out an action under the code-name of check-point 91 throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and in that action they acted together with the members of the army, JNA at the time, and the members of the federal SUP, and they controlled entry and exit motor vehicles, transportation of military equipment and so on?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that operation, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Your Honour. Could we have a date for this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Check-point 91.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. I mean, when in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was throughout 1991. We heard testimony about it in this case. I seek to have this document admitted, if there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D412, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, now that we are talking about check-points, let us touch upon another issue. 1D04-9045. It is also a document that you used in your report, the same footnote, 333, but C. Tab number 10. It is an order by the command of the 5th Corps dated 9th of May, 1992. Are you familiar with this document? It is mentioned in your report.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'd have to read it again. Unfortunately, there's a rather large number of footnotes in my -- my document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I see the second page, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can he have the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it now, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Can we have page one again. This is an order by the command of the 5th Corps signed by the commander Momir Talic. It was still called the 5th Corps at that time, and after that it was called the 1st Krajina Corps. It relates to movements of civilian vehicles in the zone of responsibility, and this order comes from the archive of the command. And it says, third paragraph: "Military police organs and mixed forces of military police and the MUP are controlling and regulating traffic at junctions and check-points." And that pertains to the zone of responsibility of the 5th Corps. You also spoke about this, about the fact that the members of the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Krajina took part in some combat operations together with the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I was referring to MUP Krajina police in the corridor a lot later than this. Here they're referring to, I'm assuming because the corps still had a component in Western Slavonia, they're referring to MUP and military police in the Western Slavonia or Krajina area that the corps deployed. So the references to the MUP of the SR Krajina but, yes, I talked in a different context about the MUP Krajina being involved in combat operations in the corridor later in 1992. I'm not aware of what operations may have been conducted by the corps and MUP Krajina in Krajina in 1991 and early 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document dated the 9th of May, and in the very first very sentence, it says: "In the zone of responsibility of the 5th Corps." It doesn't say north from Sava river, as we found in some other cases, it pertains to the whole zone of responsibility of the 5th Corps. And then in the third paragraph it says: "Controlling and regulating shall be carried out by military police organs and mixed forces of military police and the police of the Serbian Republic of Krajina." Do you agree with that? There is no specific instruction that this should be in force only in that part of the zone of responsibility of the 5th Corps which is in the territory of Croatia. This pertains to the whole zone of responsibility of the 5th Corps. Isn't that so? That's what you can conclude from this document.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is an ambiguity but it does have a wide distribution so it may well be -- I mean, the focus seems to be a problem in -- in -- in the Krajina area. He is not -- he doesn't, I don't think I would have to check again, he doesn't mention the MUP in Bosnia. But he does mention the MUP in Krajina. But the order does say "zone of responsibility," and it is a wide distribution, so he may be talking about all his units in the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, to be absolutely clear, the police of the Serbian Republic of Krajina has absolutely nothing to do with the MUP of Republika Srpska. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It's not an area, a relationship between the two is -- is not -- is not one I know well. But I am aware that Mr. Martic and, you know, was present in many meetings in 1992, but it's not an area of my expertise that I'm aware, in terms of the relationship between the two police organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So let us clarify this. The police of the Serbian Republic of Krajina is the police that comes from a part of the Republic of Croatia and which was headed by Mr. Martic. Isn't that so? That's the police of the Serbian Republic of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, since they were members of the police, they had the police uniforms. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I would assume so. But, again, I can only say that I'm not an expert on the MUP of the SRK.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to have this document admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D413, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, another document related to the same topic. It's 65 ter 10219. Your footnote 352. And tab 11. This is a memo from the command of the 1st Krajina Corps dated the 10th of June addressed to the MUP of the Republika Srpska Krajina. You have obviously seen that document before because it forms a part of your report. And in it, the command of the 1st Krajina Corps refers to a cable of the 8th of June, in which the MUP of the Serbian Krajina informs them that they had formed the volunteers unit and sent to the complement of the 1st Krajina Corps, and now Mr. Talic tells them that they will receive the unit on the 10th June at 1500 hours at the Manjaca training ground. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So this means that within the 1st Krajina Corps there was at least one unit of the MUP of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, at least from the 10th of June 1992 onwards.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I assume that MUP Krajina passed some instructions to the Main Staff saying, We have some volunteers that would be willing to come to Bosnia, and that was passed to the corps. And the corps said We're happy to have you, and you will be escorted here, and you can have some training at Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But, sir, let us be very precise. It doesn't say here, We have some volunteers. They say, We have formed a volunteers unit and are sending it into your complement, the complement of the 1st Krajina Corps. That's what is says here?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I suspect they offered that unit up and it's been agreed and accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So let us now return to the issue of the resubordination. The MUP of the Serbian Republic of Krajina forms a volunteers unit and sends it to the 1st Krajina Corps, saying, We are sending these volunteers unit into your complement. So we assume that those people wear police uniforms and they are members of the MUP of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. And now, on the 10th of June, the 1st Krajina Corps accepts this unit, and they say that they are going to take it and escort it and deploy it into the -- in the planned sector, so you would agree that now this unit becomes a part of the 1st Krajina Corps, a military formation?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the issue of uniforms I can't comment on, whether they were given combat uniforms by the corps I would imagine they were. I don't know from this document what any agreements would be in relation to the use of that volunteer unit. It may well have been that this is similar to one of the paramilitary instructions which discusses, you know, having volunteers integrated into the army, but clearly this volunteer unit is placed in the corps as a unit of the corps. Whether they were dispersed, whether they were kept as a volunteer formation, I can't say. But it's clear that the MUP RSK have offered this formation up, it's been agreed and accepted by the Main Staff, and they've been -- or they are to be integrated into the 1st Krajina Corps. How that unit was used, what that agreement was, what happened to the individuals in it, whether they stayed as a formed unit or -- I can't say. But I accept your assumption that these units are to be made available and placed in the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, those people, although they are policemen of the Serbian Republic of Krajina, when they were part of the 1st Krajina Corps, they became soldiers of the 1st Krajina Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They most probably did. I can't say for sure because I don't what agreements were there, but they may -- most probably were volunteers who were happy to come and fight presumably --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we admit this document as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Does it have to be separately admitted? It's a footnote to the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think it's on our 65 ter list, though, and your order was we could only admit documents which were on our 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D414, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I'm -- just in order to be clear about the significance of this last document that we admitted into evidence, because I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I was unsure about what it was you really wanted to prove here. Is it the Defence position that these volunteers were resubordinated, or -- or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. Absolutely, Your Honour. This is a police unit which was sent from the territory of another country. It has nothing do with Republika Srpska. So the MUP of this other country offered to the 1st Krajina Corps their own unit, police unit, which would arrive there as volunteers. They came as volunteers and they were resubordinated to the 1st Krajina Corps and, in that moment, they became soldiers. I say that this is a general principle. Every time when members of the police, regardless of whether they are volunteers or regular members, are resubordinated, they become soldiers. They cannot be, at the same time, both soldiers and policemen. When they are resubordinated, they are soldiers and they have all rights and duties as any other soldier, and this is the position of the Defence. We give this as an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, if they come from another country, can they come as policemen? I mean, they are not policemen in the RS they come as civilians in the RS and they are volunteers in -- in the RS army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I absolutely agree with you, Your Honour. Absolutely agree. The legal principle remains unchanged. It doesn't matter whether it's volunteers or whether it is a resubordination in order to carry out a certain combat task. We've seen it defined in regulations, and we are certainly going to explain that to the Chamber in more detail. And I also think that it is important to bear in mind that there is also such a thing as a volunteer unit wearing police uniforms, a unit that carries out combat activities in the territory of Republika Srpska, at least from the 10th of June 1992 and which has absolutely nothing to do with any of the accused.
